extracted.intended_audience: University legal counsel, technology transfer offices, faculty inventors, and university administrators involved in IP/commercialization
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether business-method or software-related inventions qualify as patent-eligible subject matter under U.S. law following the Supreme Court's Alice v. CLS Bank decision and related Mayo test guidance. Useful for drafting, prosecuting, and evaluating patent claims and considering alternative IP protection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent-eligibility under Section 101 (Mayo/Alice test)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court applied the patent-eligibility test described in Mayo v. Prometheus (2012) and concluded that: (1) Alice’s patent claims are directed to patent-ineligible abstract ideas; and (2) implementing those ideas on a computer was not sufficient to transform them into patent-eligible inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim is directed to an abstract idea it is ineligible for patent protection under 35 U.S.C. § 101. Review claim scope to determine whether it is 'directed to' an abstract idea and whether any additional elements transform the claim into patent-eligible subject matter under Mayo/Alice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not rely on mere computer implementation to make an abstract idea patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: Implementing abstract ideas 'on a computer' is not sufficient to transform them into patent-eligible inventions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid drafting claims that simply add generic computer functions to conventional abstract concepts. The Alice decision invalidated patents that attempted to gain protection over abstract ideas merely by adding a computer to perform generic computer functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite more than routine or conventional activity (avoid 'egregious' abstract-software claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invalidated patents in Alice were commonly regarded as relatively egregious examples of trying to use the patent system to gain protection over abstract ideas merely by adding a computer to perform generic computer functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasize specific, non-abstract technical improvements, inventive concept, or concrete practical applications in claims and specification rather than high-level business concepts or routine data-processing steps. Use claim language that shows how the invention improves computer/technical operation where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Business methods and software can still be patentable if they meet the Supreme Court's test
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-Alice, it is still possible to obtain a patent on business methods (or, more broadly, software), provided that the claimed invention meets the Supreme Court’s patent-eligibility test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting software/business-method inventions, apply the Mayo/Alice framework to demonstrate that claims are directed to patent-eligible subject matter — e.g., show an inventive concept or technical solution beyond an abstract idea plus generic computer implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consult USPTO post-Alice examiner guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: In response to Alice, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office has issued additional guidelines to its patent examiners (link provided).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Review the USPTO guidance (http://www.uspto.gov/patents/announce/alice_pec_25jun2014.pdf) to understand how examiners are instructed to apply the Alice/Mayo framework in practice and to align claim drafting and prosecution strategy with examiner expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider alternative IP protection such as copyright for software
rubrics_metrics.description: Intellectual property owners may continue to rely on copyright law to protect, license and enforce similar business methods so long as the underlying software code contains sufficient copyrightable expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If patent protection is unlikely (e.g., claims deemed abstract), evaluate whether the implementation's source code, user interface, or expressive elements qualify for copyright protection and whether licensing, trade secret, or other strategies are appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Technical/non-abstract inventions are less likely to be affected
rubrics_metrics.description: Much of the University’s patent portfolio consists of inventions that are not directly implicated by the type of business methods at issue in Alice – e.g., non-abstract advances in medical, veterinary, clean water, and energy technologies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Focus patenting efforts on concrete technical improvements and non-abstract advances in science and engineering fields, which are less vulnerable to Section 101 challenges of the type addressed in Alice.
